newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICAN INSURER WANTS CLAIMANTS TO PASS LIE TESTS.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICAN INSURER WANTS CLAIMANTS TO PASS LIE TESTS.

text.p: With a torrent of fraudulent claims flooding the insurance industry in crime-hit South Africa, one company wants its clients to pass lie detector tests before it will pay claims.

Multifund Insurance Brokers (MFI) managing director Cornelius van Heerden said on Wednesday 12 clients had submitted to lie-detector or polygraph tests in the past year, saving the firm about 500,000 ($109,000) rand in fraudulent claims.

South African law courts do not accept polygraph findings and because the tests were not written into the insurance contracts the evidence would be inconclusive if clients chose to take legal action, van Heerden told Reuters.
But out of the dozen tested, 11 clients dropped their claims after the polygraphs showed they had been lying.
Testing mainly involved short-term insurance claims covering household goods or motor vehicles.
The company has now made lie-detector tests a condition of all its insurance contracts, so potential clients know what they will be up against if they have to prove a disputed claim.
"A person wanting to take insurance from us must now be willing to take the test and agree to abide by its outcome," van Heerden said.
Long-term clients of good standing were exempted from the 450 rand ($98) test.
"We have received a good response from our clients who feel by this we will pass to them low premiums on their insurance if the company is able to crack down on fraudulent claims," he said.
The test had shown success rates of 90 to 96 percent by insurers in India, Israel and the United States. It did not falsely accuse honest people, but every now and then a guilty person got through.
Lala Camerer, a researcher looking into commercial crime and fraud in South Africa, said insurance companies "are really being taken for a ride by some of their clients".

Polygraph testing might deter some faudsters who inflated claims or claimed for things they had not lost, but it remained "ethically problematic", said Camerer, who works at the independent Institute for Defence Policy.
"The problem is that the general public are not made fully aware of what they are in for. The small print is a problem," Camerer added.
Recent figures released by South African police put the cost of commercial crime at over 1.1 billion rand in the first four months of the year.

The figure compared with over 1.3 billion rand over the same period in 1995 and 1.9 billion rand in the corresponding period in 1994. While the figures were slightly down police said the battle against fraud was still a long way from being won.
